Job #42 has finished training. The scheduler tells AutoResearch that the job used 0.6 GPU-hours. The controller asks the evaluator to score the trained model. Ten minutes pass. No score arrives. Should AutoResearch start the next trial?

Remember why the model in [Block 1](01-agent-fundamentals.qmd) tried a second seed. It saw a promising result and wanted to check whether the gain would repeat. Here the evaluator might already have that result. If the controller gives the model another turn now, the model will choose from the baseline score alone, and the first trial will still be on the books.

It should keep the trial pending and look up the score it already requested. To do that, the controller needs to remember what it is waiting for and which replies would justify a next step. Give “waiting for a score” a name, *Scoring*. Write one rule for receiving the score and another for reaching the time limit. A set of named situations and rules like these is a **state machine**. We’ll follow one trial through it twice. The training run and its score will be the same both times. What changes is when the controller learns the score.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this block fits

Block 1 gave the model a choice of experiments and the runtime the final say over which ones can run. Here you build the controller that keeps track of an approved trial until it is settled. The [AutoResearch case study](../case-studies/autoresearch.qmd#building-autoresearch-block-by-block) follows this design through the rest of the course.
:::

## The controller at a glance

In Figure 1, select **Dispatching**, then **Running**. What new fact would justify moving from the first box to the second? The scheduler has to acknowledge the request. The controller may have already sent it while the run is still in Dispatching. An arrow represents permission to move when particular evidence arrives.

::: {#fig-controller-overview}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/controller-overview.html >}}

```

The AutoResearch controller in one picture. Select a mode or a group to read what happens there, or select an event source to light the edges it can fire.

:::

Follow the center of the diagram once. In *Ready*, the controller checks the limits. In *Proposing*, the model gets a turn. In *Authorizing*, the gate checks the proposal. Follow the trial down to *Scoring* and back to *Ready*. That return matters. Even after a good result, the controller checks the limits before it gives the model another turn.

Two detours explain the other boxes. If a reply is overdue, the controller enters *Reconciling* to find out what happened. If an operator cancels, it enters *Stopped*, freezes the current best candidate (the **incumbent**), and settles any pending trial. The fixed evaluator then scores the frozen selection on held-back data. Recording that final score takes the run to *Done*.

## Learning objectives

By the end, you should be able to read one arrow as a sentence, explain what a saved record lets the controller know after a crash, and decide whether a missing reply calls for waiting, looking up a result, or repeating a request. You’ll apply the same reasoning to a coding agent that edits its own training script.

## 1. When a loop stops being enough

Picture a loop that tries four numbers from a list. It calls a scoring function, compares the answer with the best so far, and advances to the next number. The loop index and two local variables are enough for the course’s small AutoResearch lab. Each call finishes before the next one starts, and rerunning the experiment is cheap.

Now move training onto another machine. Suppose the controller sends a request and its process crashes. The scheduler can keep running the job. After a restart, “go back to the line that sends the request” could launch two jobs. The controller needs a saved record of the approved request and a rule for finding out whether the scheduler has it.

### Terms used in this lesson

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Terms used in the lesson"}

| Think of job #42 | Name in the lesson |
|---|---|
| The controller is waiting for the scheduler to acknowledge a request. | **Mode** — *Dispatching* in this case. |
| A saved entry names the pending trial, its request ID, and its compute reservation. | **Ledger** — the facts the controller uses to make decisions. The **controller record** combines the mode and the ledger. |
| The scheduler replies that it accepted the request. | **Event** — a message or occurrence the controller handles. |
| Does the reply name the pending request? | **Guard** — a condition the controller checks before acting. |
| Save the job number the scheduler returned. | **Update** — a change to the ledger. |
| In Dispatching, on a matching acknowledgement, save the job number and enter Running. | **Transition** — one rule connecting a mode, an event, a guard, an update, and a next mode. |
| Save the mode and ledger so a new process can recover them. | **Checkpoint** — a durable, numbered copy of the controller record at a transition boundary. |

:::

The controller gives the submission an **operation ID** before sending it. Later it gives the scoring request a **scoring ID**. Each service can use its ID to find the original request and recognize a repeat. The scheduler also supplies its own **job ID** once it accepts the submission.

There are nine modes, even though the ledger can hold many different job IDs and scores. The technical name for this combination is an *extended finite-state machine*. Figure 1 groups modes that share a rule. For example, an operator can cancel from any mode in the *Search* group. Grouping them lets us draw that rule once. Harel developed this idea in statecharts [@harel1987statecharts].

## 2. Who produces each event

When a message arrives, ask who could know the fact it reports. The model can suggest seed 7. The scheduler can say whether a worker ran it. The evaluator can say how well the trained candidate scored.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Event sources"}

| Source | What arrives | What the controller checks or does |
|---|---|---|
| Model and its decoder | A proposal, a request to stop, or an unusable or overdue reply | Accept a reply only for the current policy turn. Count an unusable reply against the proposal limit. |
| Gate | Approval or rejection | Bind approval to the exact arguments the gate checked. |
| Scheduler | A job acknowledgement, completion, failure, or lookup result | Match the report to the pending work before changing its record. |
| Evaluator | A score, including one retrieved from storage | Check the trial and evaluator version before comparing scores. |
| Clock, operator, process host | A timeout, deadline, cancellation, or restart | Apply the rule for the current mode. The host is the supervisor that restarts the controller. |
| Controller | A check of the run’s limits | Start another policy turn or stop the search. |

:::

The runtime can decline a proposal. It cannot undo a completed job by declining to read the message. It needs a way to handle accurate reports, duplicates, and reports that arrive after the search has stopped.

## 3. The worked controller

The figures use the schematic values from the [controller lab](../labs/index.qmd#the-controller-as-a-transition-table). Run `python -m labs.controller --scenario ordinary` to follow the first trial or use `--scenario lost-score` to follow its recovery.

Start with the baseline at **0.842**. Higher validation scores win in this example. Evaluator v1 scores every candidate, and a tie keeps the incumbent. The run has **2.0 GPU-hours**, **5 trials**, **10 proposals**, and a deadline. The smallest allowed trial estimate is 0.3 GPU-hours. The scheduler caps each job at the amount reserved for it.

A rejection uses a proposal. Approval uses a trial and reserves compute before the request goes out. A trial can use at most two scoring requests and three recovery attempts. These limits also cover cases where useful work never finishes. The holdout stays sealed until the search stops and every pending trial has been settled.

As you step through Figure 2, follow an approved proposal. Pause when row 7 sends it. What would a restarted controller need to ask the scheduler at this point?

::: {#fig-controller-states}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/controller-states.html >}}

```

Rows 1–13 of the controller, added in the order a run meets them. Each step shows one row: its mode, event, guard, update, and next mode.

:::

### The transition table

Read a row from left to right. First find where the controller is. Then identify who sent the event, check whether it belongs to this trial, and read what the controller records before it moves.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Reading three transition rows"}

| Current mode | Event | Guard | Update | Next mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dispatching | Scheduler accepts a job | Operation ID matches the pending submission | Save the scheduler’s job ID | Running |
| Running | Scheduler reports completion | Job ID matches the pending job | Record the reported cost and request a score under the trial’s scoring ID | Scoring |
| Scoring | Evaluator returns a score | Score is for the pending trial and comes from v1 | Charge the cost, release the reservation, apply the comparison rule, and close the trial | Ready |

:::

Try the first row with two different messages. “Accepted your request, job #42” takes the controller to Running **if the request ID matches**. An acknowledgement for yesterday’s submission fails that check. The controller logs the unmatched event and keeps waiting. The guard makes that difference explicit.

**Why save before sending?** Once the submission leaves the controller, the scheduler can start work even if its acknowledgement never gets back. Row 7 therefore saves the trial ID, operation ID, exact approved arguments, and reservation in a checkpoint before it sends anything. After a crash, those entries give the controller both a question (“Have you seen this operation ID?”) and the exact request it may need to resend. A crash before that checkpoint leaves the request unsent.

The model chooses between proposing a trial and asking to stop. The gate can reject a proposal, and an unusable reply consumes a proposal. All three paths eventually return to Ready, where the controller checks its limits. Cancellation and the deadline can stop the search immediately from any search mode.

## 4. Formalizing the controller

Return to row 8. Just before the scheduler’s acknowledgement, the mode is Dispatching and the ledger holds the operation ID. Just after a matching acknowledgement, the mode is Running and the ledger also holds job #42. The equation below describes that single change. You can read the rest of the lesson with the same five columns you just used.

Call the incoming acknowledgement event $\sigma_n$. The subscript $n$ counts **events**. Write $q$ for the mode, $\ell$ for the ledger, and $z=(q,\ell)$ for the complete record. For a rule $r$, read the tests to the right of “if” first. Is the current mode in its allowed set $Q_r$? Is this kind of event in $K_r$? Does its guard $G_r$ pass?

$$
(q_n,\ell_n)=(q'_r,f_r(\ell_{n-1},\sigma_n))
\quad\text{if}\quad
q_{n-1}\in Q_r,\quad \kappa(\sigma_n)\in K_r,\quad G_r(\ell_{n-1},\sigma_n).
$$

Here $\kappa$ gives the event type. On the left, $q'_r$ is the destination and $f_r$ updates the ledger. In row 8, those mean “enter Running” and “save #42.” With no matching rule the controller logs the event and keeps its record. Some rows also deliberately keep the same mode. Rows 20 and 23 each group two related rules.

Call the operation of processing one event $\delta$. Processing two events in order gives $z_2=\delta(\delta(z_0,\sigma_1),\sigma_2)$. Each record and event enable at most one rule. Given the same starting record and the same ordered events, the controller will rebuild the same decisions. This is **deterministic replay**. During replay it reads the recorded model reply, acknowledgement, or score. Calling the model again could give a different answer.

Block 1 counted **model turns**. Several events here can pass between turns. At event $n_k$, when the controller enters Proposing for turn $k$, it builds context $c_k=\phi(g,z_{n_k})$ from the goal and the record. The model chooses from the operations offered in that context, $\tilde a_k\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid c_k,\mathcal A_k^{\mathrm{avail}})$. Its reply carries turn number $k$. Evidence already reached the ledger through earlier events, so context building can use the record alone. The gate’s verdict, the scheduler’s report, and the stop check from Block 1 now have their own rows. An outside action can take effect before the controller learns its outcome.

Five promises should still hold after **every** row. These are the controller’s *invariants*.

- **One trial at a time.** The ledger has one pending slot. Even a stopped search can have one trial left to settle.
- **Close once.** Closing requires a matching pending trial. In one update the controller charges its cost, releases its reservation, moves its ID to the closed set, and clears the slot. A duplicate cannot charge or promote it again.
- **No new trials after a stop.** The controller freezes the incumbent. Late evidence can settle a bill, but there is no route from Stopped back to Proposing.
- **Stay within budget.** Spent plus reserved compute stays within 2.0 GPU-hours. If the cost remains unknown after recovery is exhausted, the controller charges the full reservation. The scheduler’s cap makes that a valid upper bound.
- **Keep the holdout sealed.** Only the final transition records the holdout score, after selection is frozen and no trial is pending.

Why have a proposal limit as well as a trial limit? Imagine a model that keeps proposing forbidden jobs. It could spend all afternoon doing so without using a single trial. Limits on proposals, trials, scoring, and recovery bound the work. Timers matter too. A waiting controller needs an event before it can act. The deadline ends the search. Reaching Done still requires the final holdout result. A production controller also needs a timeout and retry policy for that final request.

## 5. Systems connections

- **Supervisory control.** The controller can block an unapproved submission. It cannot block the passage of time or prevent a late score from arriving. This is why we ask how each mode handles events outside its control. [@ramadge1987supervisory]
- **State-machine replication.** Two copies of a deterministic controller agree if they start together and process the same events in the same order. One controller recovering tomorrow can use the same idea. Record the deadline as an event so replay uses the original timing decision. [@schneider1990statemachine]
- **Decisions at different timescales.** The model chooses a trial once. Several minutes of training, waiting, and bookkeeping can pass before it chooses again. To evaluate those choices, keep the duration and cost between them. This connects the example to semi-Markov decisions. [@sutton1999options]
- **ReAct.** In the paper’s search tasks, the model can choose to search, look something up, or finish. Here it can propose a trial or ask to stop. The surrounding software owns promotion and enforces hard stops. The available choices determine how much of the loop the model controls. [@yao2023react]

## 6. Trace 1 — An ordinary trial

Choose **Ordinary trial** in Figure 3. Watch the *Pending* field. When does the controller first know that the scheduler has job #42? When does it have enough evidence to keep the candidate?

::: {#fig-controller-trace}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/controller-trace.html >}}

```

Three runs of trial t1. Each step shows the row that fired, where the run is, and what changed in the controller record, external state, and policy context.

:::

1. **The model proposes seed 7.** The gate approves the settings. The controller saves the request as `t1-submit`, counts trial `t1`, and reserves 0.7 GPU-hours. **Checkpoint 3** establishes those facts. The submission may already have left the process. Whether the scheduler received it is still open.
2. **The scheduler acknowledges job #42.** The operation ID matches `t1-submit`, so the controller saves the job ID at **checkpoint 4**. That proves it received an acknowledgement. A job can finish while the controller is offline, so this checkpoint alone cannot tell a restarted controller whether the job is still running.
3. **The scheduler reports that training finished.** The cost was 0.6 GPU-hours. The controller records that cost and requests a score under `t1-score`. At **checkpoint 5** the reservation still covers the trial. The incumbent is still the baseline.
4. **Evaluator v1 returns 0.851 for t1.** It beats 0.842. In one update the controller promotes t1, charges 0.6, releases the 0.7 reservation, and closes t1. **Checkpoint 6** records that decision. The balance is 1.4 GPU-hours, and the trial has been charged once.
5. **The controller checks the limits again.** There is room for another trial. This time the model sees the new incumbent and proposes seed 11 to see whether the gain repeats.

## 7. Trace 2 — A lost score reply

Switch @fig-controller-trace to **Lost score reply** and pause at step 7. Everything through checkpoint 5 is the same. This time the evaluator saves 0.851, but the controller has heard nothing after ten minutes. You can see the score in the evaluator’s panel. Cover that panel and read only the controller’s record. What evidence does it actually have?

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Evidence at the scoring timeout"}

| At the timeout | What it means for the next decision |
|---|---|
| The scheduler confirmed job #42 finished at a cost of 0.6 GPU-hours. | Training is complete. Repeating training would spend compute on work already done. |
| The ledger names the scoring request, `t1-score`. | The controller knows exactly which result to ask the evaluator for. It cannot infer the score from silence. |
| The trial is pending, with 0.7 GPU-hours reserved. | The controller must settle t1 before it gives the model another turn. Its outcome could change what the model proposes. |

:::

**Look up the request that might already have succeeded.** On timeout, row 14 enters Reconciling and keeps the reservation. The controller asks the evaluator for the stored result under `t1-score` and can use `t1-submit` to check the scheduler’s record. The evaluator returns 0.851 from v1 for the pending trial. The cost is already known, so row 16 can make exactly the decision row 11 made in the ordinary run. The controller promotes t1, charges 0.6, releases 0.7, and closes the trial.

Now advance one step. The overdue reply finally arrives. The pending slot is empty and t1 is closed, so row 22 logs the reply. The balance is still 1.4. Charging every incoming score would have deducted 0.6 twice. The two runs took different paths to the same evidence for the model’s next turn.

**What if the lookup gives another answer?** The controller uses the IDs it saved before making the requests. The following choices assume the search is active and recovery attempts remain.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Recovery decisions"}

| Evidence from the services | Next step |
|---|---|
| Job finished, and the evaluator has no stored score | If a scoring attempt remains, request scoring under the **same scoring ID** (row 17). The evaluator must recognize a repeat and return any result it has stored. A fresh ID could create two different scores for one trial. When scoring attempts are exhausted, charge the known cost and close unresolved (row 18). |
| Scheduler says the job is running | Save or confirm the job identity and resume waiting (row 20). |
| No acknowledgement was recorded and the scheduler finds no job for the operation ID | Resend the exact stored submission with the **same operation ID** (row 20). The scheduler must recognize both copies as one job even if the first request arrives late. |
| Scheduler reports that the job failed | Charge the reported cost and close without promotion (row 19). |
| Evidence is still missing or inconsistent | Keep the trial pending while recovery attempts remain. When none remain, request cancellation, charge the full reservation, and close unresolved (row 15). |

:::

Looking up a result reads what already happened. Repeating a request can cause work. A retry is safe here because the service recognizes the original ID, the request still describes the same work, and the controller checks the remaining attempts. An empty lookup on its own cannot provide that guarantee.

**Try Cancel mid-run.** An operator cancels while #42 is running. Row 12 freezes the baseline and asks the scheduler to cancel. The scheduler later reports it spent 0.4 GPU-hours. Row 23 charges 0.4, releases the reservation, and closes t1 without promotion. Now the evaluator can score the frozen baseline on the holdout. Even with 1.6 GPU-hours left, the model gets no further turn. If the report never comes, the stopped controller can settle at the reservation on timeout.

**Try a restart on paper.** If the process dies in Scoring, the host restarts it and the controller recovers the saved scoring ID. It follows the same lookup rules. A crash during Proposing loses a model call, which row 21 counts against the proposal limit. A crash during Authorizing lets the deterministic gate recheck the proposal already on record.

## 8. Controller record, external state, and context

Stay at the timeout in Figure 3. Three panels tell three different stories about the same moment.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Three kinds of state"}

| Where you look | What you see | Who can change it? |
|---|---|---|
| Controller record ($z$) | The baseline leads at 0.842. Trial t1 is pending, with 0.7 GPU-hours reserved and a score requested. | The controller updates the ledger when a rule fires. It restores this record after a restart. |
| External state ($x$) | The scheduler has finished #42. The evaluator already holds 0.851. | The scheduler, workers, and evaluator change their own records. The controller learns about them through reports and lookups. |
| Policy context ($c$) | The last prompt still shows the original baseline and budget. | The runtime builds a context when the model gets a turn. It will rebuild the next one from the ledger after checking the limits. |

:::

Each panel answers a different question. To decide whether a new trial is legal, consult the controller record. To find a measured score, ask the evaluator. To explain why the model proposed another seed, inspect what it saw on that turn.

## 9. Loop, table, or graph engine

Imagine making just one change to the four-number lab. Move scoring onto a service that might answer after the calling process restarts. The search objective stays the same. What changes is the work the controller must remember.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Implementation choices"}

| Choose | When it earns its place |
|---|---|
| A plain loop | Each call completes in the same process, side effects end with that process, and restarting from the beginning is cheap. A handful of local variables captures progress. |
| A transition table and a small driver loop | Jobs outlive a call, results can arrive late, or the team needs to explain why it approved or retried a particular request. Rows make those decisions inspectable and testable. |
| A durable-workflow or graph engine | The team also needs durable timers, many concurrent runs, long pauses for approval, parallel branches, or migration of running workflows. Compare the cost of maintaining those features with the constraints of the engine. |

:::

An engine still needs a safe submission rule. A LangGraph node can run again when an interrupted workflow resumes. Temporal replays workflow history and puts outside work in activities. Amazon States Language lets a task declare retry and catch rules. In each design, ask what the training service will do if it sees the same launch twice. [@langgraph2026interrupts; @temporal2026workflowdefinition; @aws2026stateslanguage]

## 10. Failure modes

Read each symptom and identify the first point where the controller accepted too little evidence.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Failure modes"}

| What went wrong | What would have prevented it? |
|---|---|
| A restart loses the only mention of a pending job. | Save the pending request in the controller record before sending it. The model’s conversation is a poor place to recover a job ID. |
| The model writes “promote t1” and the ledger records a win. | Require a score from the designated evaluator for the pending trial. |
| A timeout launches a second job, or the system retries forever. | Look up the original operation, require the service to deduplicate a permitted resend, and bound the attempts. |
| A scoring reply is lost and the system waits indefinitely. | Give Scoring a timeout and a rule that starts recovery. |
| The gate approved seed 7, but the worker runs seed 11. | Bind approval to the exact arguments sent to the worker. |
| Replay yields a different decision. | Record the inputs that affected the decision, including model replies and clock events. |
| Rejected proposals consume an afternoon, or a second route to the model skips the budget check. | Count proposals as well as trials, and start every policy turn from Ready after checking the limits. |

:::

## 11. Production implications

To test a controller, take a real sequence of events and change one thing. Deliver the same score twice. Restart just after the approval checkpoint. Cancel while the job is running. Check the five invariants after **each** step. Also check every mode against events it might receive, including events it should simply log and ignore.

For each decision, record the event, its IDs, the row that fired, its update, and the destination. If an operator asks why trial 2 started late, that log can show how long trial 1 spent waiting for a score and how many lookups it needed. It also lets the team distinguish a rejected proposal from a lost scheduler reply.

Keep the table version with the run. A controller restarted on Tuesday needs to know which rules governed Monday’s decisions. If several trials will run at once, give each its own record and define when their results can be combined. This lesson’s single pending slot assumes one trial at a time.

## 12. Applying the design to the real AutoResearch loop

So far the model chose settings such as a seed. In [Karpathy’s AutoResearch at commit 228791f](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch/tree/228791f) [@karpathy2026autoresearch], a coding agent can change the training program itself. Follow one candidate from code edit to decision. The left side of Figure 4 shows the published project. The right side shows the course’s proposed redesign, with illustrative limits.

### The loop as written

The agent edits `train.py`, commits its change, and runs training. The training code budgets five minutes for training, and the instructions tell the agent to kill a run that takes longer than ten minutes. The agent reads validation bits per byte (`val_bpb`) from `run.log`. Here **lower is better**. If training crashes, the agent reads the error and may try to fix the code.

The agent records the commit, metric, peak memory, outcome, and description in `results.tsv`, outside Git. An improvement keeps the candidate commit. An equal or worse score sends the branch back to its starting commit. The instructions also ask the agent to weigh code simplicity and to keep experimenting until a person interrupts it. A simpler change with an equal score shows why someone designing a controller must choose an explicit keep rule.

### Step 1 — Read the implicit state machine

Picture the person checking the GPU the next morning. They find a candidate commit, a partial log, and no result for that commit. Can they tell whether training ever started? The missing fact lived in the agent’s session. Git identifies the code and the log records some output, but neither one establishes the trial’s current status.

::: {#fig-controller-upstream}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/controller-upstream.html >}}

```

One upstream experiment, rule by rule. Each step moves a rule from the agent to what enforces it in the redesign, or shows a choice the agent keeps.

:::

In the left lane, notice who both proposes the experiment and reads its result. The agent edits `train.py`, which supplies the model’s forward pass and loss, prints the score, and contains the five-minute training break. The project keeps the data loader and evaluation function in `prepare.py`, yet the training code can influence what gets measured and can request validation data. The redesign has to decide which facts the controller can trust when it selects a winner.

### Step 2 — Decide which transitions become explicit

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Decisions in the AutoResearch redesign"}

| Decision in this experiment | Who owns it in the redesign, and why? |
|---|---|
| Which change or repair is worth a trial? | The model proposes a patch or a fix against the incumbent. It can also ask to stop. These choices use what it has learned from earlier results. |
| May this exact patch run? | The gate checks the diff and binds approval to its hash. Only `train.py` may change, no packages may be added, and the pinned data/evaluation file and lock file must match. The gate allows three fixes per idea. Since the model labels each idea, the overall trial cap supplies the firm bound. |
| How long can training use the GPU? | A process host enforces a seven-minute wall-clock cap in this redesign. This allows startup and saving around a five-minute training budget. A patch could remove the training break and use the allowance, so exact training-time equality would require a timer in fixed code. |
| Who measures improvement? | Training saves weights and has no access to the validation or holdout shard. An evaluator at a fixed code version checks that changing later tokens leaves earlier predictions unchanged. It computes bits per byte from the model’s outputs. Candidate code still runs during evaluation. |
| Which commit should the branch point to? | The controller keeps a candidate only for a strictly lower validation score. It saves that decision before pointing the branch at the selected commit. If the team wants to reward simpler code, it must define a measurable rule and a tolerance grounded in evaluation noise. |
| What happens to the results file? | The controller generates one row per closed trial from the ledger. Regenerating the file after a crash produces the same report. |
| When does the search end? | The controller enforces 60 trials or 120 proposals. A person can cancel, and an eight-hour deadline can end the search. The evaluator scores the frozen winner once on a separately reserved holdout shard. |

:::

### Step 3 — Rewrite the rows that change

Suppose the model proposes a patch. Row 3 records the diff and whether the model calls it a new idea or a fix. The gate checks it against the current winning commit, called the **base commit**. If the gate approves, row 7 creates a **candidate commit** from that base and patch on a separate Git reference. The controller saves both commit IDs, assigns a run ID, spends one trial, and reserves one run slot. Only after that checkpoint does it ask the host to launch. The winning branch still points to the incumbent.

When the host reports success, row 9 checks the run ID, a zero exit status, and the presence of saved weights before requesting evaluation. A nonzero exit, missing weights, or the host’s seven-minute kill closes the trial as a crash under row 10. The controller keeps the patch and log tail so the model can propose a repair. A failed causality check also closes the trial without promotion. A separate, longer controller timeout detects a missing host report even after the host’s time limit has passed.

The pinned evaluator scores the saved weights. If the result for the pending trial is strictly lower than the incumbent’s, row 11 records the candidate as the winner. Row 16 applies the same update if the controller recovers the result by lookup. The controller then sets the branch to the recorded winner. Repeating “set the branch to this commit” after a restart leads to the same branch head.

### Step 4 — Trace an ambiguous outcome and check the invariants

Trial `t7` was in flight when the controller restarted. This time the saved record identifies which patch the gate approved, which candidate commit the host was asked to train, and which run ID to look up. The launch checkpoint establishes what the controller saved. To learn what the GPU did, the controller asks the host about **`t7-run`** and checks the evaluator for any stored score.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Restart decisions for trial t7"}

| What the recovered controller learns | Why the next step is legal |
|---|---|
| The checkpoint says Dispatching, no acknowledgement was recorded, and the host finds no run under that ID. | With a recovery attempt available, resend the same candidate commit under `t7-run`. The original request could still arrive. The host must refuse a second launch with that ID. |
| The host already has the run and it is still training. | Resume waiting. The host’s original time cap still applies. |
| The host confirms successful completion and saved weights. | If a valid score is already stored and cost is known, apply the promotion rule once. If there is no score and a scoring attempt remains, request it under the original scoring ID. Exhausted scoring attempts close the trial unresolved. |
| The run failed, was killed, or produced no weights. | Charge the slot, preserve the evidence for a possible fix, and close the trial as a crash. |
| The controller has an acknowledgement, but the host can no longer find the run. | An earlier acknowledgement rules out the unacknowledged-launch resend path. Continue bounded lookups. When recovery attempts run out, request cancellation and settle the trial unresolved. |

:::

Check the five promises against this example. One pending slot tracks one trial. Closing it once gives `results.tsv` one entry. Cancellation freezes the branch selection. Sixty seven-minute slots bound training to seven GPU-hours, while the eight-hour deadline bounds search time. The holdout shard, reserved before the evaluation code is pinned, supplies one final assessment after the search stops.

For one person watching one GPU, the upstream loop lets them try an idea and inspect the result with little machinery. For an unattended night of experiments, the redesign earns its extra rules when a morning decision depends on knowing exactly which code ran, how it was measured, and whether the result was already applied.

## 13. AutoResearch after Block 02

Take the “run and score” box from Block 1. You can now open that box and say who knows what. The scheduler acknowledges a specific submission. The evaluator measures a specific trial. The controller keeps the evidence needed to choose its next legal step after a reply, a timeout, or a restart. The model still gets to choose an experiment once that evidence is ready.

The [worked lab](../labs/index.qmd#the-controller-as-a-transition-table) implements nine modes and 23 numbered rows. To follow the code, start with rows 7–11 for one ordinary trial and add rows 14, 16, and 22 for the late reply. The [next block](03-tool-use.qmd) defines the tools and request contracts that make those rows possible. [Controller lab](https://github.com/hieutrungle/agentic-systems-notes/blob/main/labs/controller.py)

## 14. Conclusion

Return to job #42. Ten minutes have passed. Training finished, the evaluator might have saved a score, and the controller has the ID of the request it sent. It can now take a useful step without guessing. It keeps the trial pending, looks up the original request, and applies a verified result once. Once the controller has closed the trial and checked the limits, the model can decide whether another seed is worth trying.

When designing your own controller, pick one arrow and fill in the blanks. “While we are waiting for \_\_\_, if \_\_\_ tells us \_\_\_ and we can verify \_\_\_, we record \_\_\_ and move to \_\_\_.” If you can fill it in, you can write the row.

## 16. Conceptual questions

1. The model writes “job #42 succeeded, promote it.” Which row can that reply fire?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   In Proposing, a reply for the current turn can propose a trial, ask to stop, or be counted as unusable by the decoder. None of those outcomes promotes a candidate. Promotion requires a matching evaluator result, delivered directly or recovered from storage.

   </details>

2. At the scoring timeout, why look up t1-score before asking the model what to try next?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   The controller knows the job finished at a cost of 0.6 GPU-hours. It knows which score it requested. It still lacks the value. Looking up the original scoring ID can recover a result already measured. Closing t1 updates the incumbent and the budget the model will see. A new scoring ID could produce a second result for the same trial.

   </details>

3. A launch checkpoint survives a crash. What else must you learn before resending?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   The checkpoint proves the controller saved the approved request, counted the trial, and reserved its compute. Look up the original operation ID. Resume waiting if the scheduler is running the job, or handle the result if it finished. A resend requires an unacknowledged submission, no job found, and a recovery attempt remaining. Send the exact stored request under the same ID to a service that deduplicates it.

   </details>

4. Why count the trial at approval? How would you test it?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   After the approval checkpoint, outside work can begin even if its reply disappears. Counting at completion would let lost replies hide work from the trial budget. Test a rejection, a crash after approval, and a duplicate score. Expect a proposal count for the rejection, one trial and reservation for the approval, and just one charge at closure.

   </details>

5. A four-candidate loop works today. What change would justify a table? What would justify an engine?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   Move scoring to a service that can outlive the caller and lose a reply. Now the controller needs an explicit rule for an uncertain outcome. A small table can do that. If the team also has to maintain durable timers, long approval waits, or many concurrent runs, a workflow engine may be worth its operating constraints.

   </details>
